title-group.article-title: Efficacy and safety of interleukin-6 receptor antagonists in adult patients admitted to intensive care unit with COVID-19: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

list-item.p: Tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) might reduce 5.76 days of ICU stay among severe or critical COVID-19 patients (Moderate certainty).
Tocilizumab and sarilumab did not increase the risk of serious adverse events among severe or critical COVID-19 patients.
Tocilizumab and sarilumab failed to reduce the all-cause mortality among severe or critical COVID-19 patients.

sec.p: Keywords: Tocilizumab, Sarilumab, COVID-19, Meta-analysis, Systematic review

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The purpose of the systematic review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6) antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) in adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19. A systematic review of the literature was conducted in Medline, Cochrane and Embase databases, and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov from the inception dates to10 January 2023. Randomized clinical trials comparing IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) with a placebo or usual care treatment for adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 were identified. Two independent reviewers performed the assessment and selection of eligible studies, assessed study quality and extracted data. Relative risk (RR), mean difference (MD), and 95% confidence interval (CI) with random-effects models was performed in meta-analysis. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to assess the quality of the evidence. The search retrieved a total of 11 RCTs involving 5028 participants were eligible for meta-analysis. Our findings suggest that as the new drug used in adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19, IL-6 antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) may reduce the length of ICU stay and hospital stay. However, they did not significantly increase the risks of serious adverse events and did not reduce all-cause mortality (28-day, 14-day, and 7-day).

sec.p: Received 2023 May 15; Revised 2023 Jun 1; Accepted 2023 Jun 3; Collection date 2023 Aug.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The COVID-19 pandemic has been a global crisis at an unprecedented level (Huang et al., 2022, Jennifer et al., 2023). The whole disease process, from symptoms and diagnosis to medications and treatment, has been a challenge, as COVID-19 is a novel disease that the world has never before encountered. Compared with other fatal diseases, the COVID-19 is an infectious disease with highly infectivity in humans, but the mortality rate is relatively low. Although critically ill cases composed around 5% of cases, their mortality rate is close to 50% (Hermine et al., 2022). The critically ill patients are heterogeneous populations (Elke et al., 2019), treatments for severe or critical COVID-19 are complex (McCreary and Meyer, 2021). The Report of the fifteenth meeting of the International Health Regulations (2005) (IHR) Emergency Committee regarding the coronavirus 2019 disease (COVID-19) pandemic, held on 4 May 2023, suggested that COVID-19 is now an established and ongoing health issue which no longer constitutes a public health emergency of international concern. However, this is not the time to stop work or dismantle systems. The Committee advocated that WHO, partners, and States Parties dedicate sustained attention and resources to preparedness and resilience for emerging threats. Furthermore, we should continue to support research to develop relevant integrated care pathways (WHO, 2005). Therefore, treatment for patients with severe COVID-19 is more important, the doctors and nurses need to work on reduce the conversion of severe cases to critical ill cases. Both the results of a prospective meta-analysis (Shankar-Hari et al., 2021) and the latest guidelines of the World Health Organization (WHO) (Lamontagne et al., 2020) suggested that the interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonists (tocilizumab and sarilumab), together with corticosteroids, have been recommended as the routine treatment for patients with COVID-19 who need oxygen support. Critical illness is usually associated with inflammation and stress response (Peng et al., 2021). Patients with COVID-19 pneumonia present nonspecific inflammatory responses (Hermine et al., 2022). Given the association of elevated IL-6 levels with severe COVID-19 and mortality, therapy with biologic agents blocking IL-6 seems to be a promising treatment for severe or critical COVID-19 (Salvarani et al., 2021). However, more recently, some randomized controlled trials (RCTs) about the efficacy and safety of IL-6 receptor antagonists in adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 have been published. Some authors have found that tocilizumab and sarilumab exerted a beneficial effect on reducing death, whereas other authors have found no effect or even a deleterious action of tocilizumab and sarilumab among adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 (Hermine et al., 2022, Veiga et al., 2021). Most notably, Viviane C Veiga et al. reported that tocilizumab plus standard care might not be better than standard care alone in improving clinical outcomes, and it might increase mortality in patients with severe or critical COVID-19 (Veiga et al., 2021). Faced with this situation, many uncertainties remain on the actual role of the IL-6 receptor antagonists among adult patients with COVID-19 require admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) (Caballero Bermejo et al., 2020). Providing timely, policy-relevant, quality research evidence is necessary to evaluate the risks and benefits of the IL-6 receptor antagonists, tocilizumab and sarilumab among severe or critical ill patients with COVID-19 (Somers et al., 2021). A systematic review of trials offers an opportunity to consider the total body of evidence and potentially resolve the concern. This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials focuses on making recommendations for the use of IL-6 receptor antagonists in this setting.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We followed the methodology of the Cochrane Handbook (version 5.1.0) (Sanchex et al., 2020) and PRISMA statement (Liberati et al., 2009). The review protocol is available on PROSPERO, registration number CRD42023392450. We performed a secondary analysis of randomly trials, our systematic review exempts from ethical compliance.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: The Medline, Cochrane and Embase databases in OVID were systematically searched from the inception dates to10 January 2023, the detailed search strategies are reported in the Supplement. We also searched the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) (http://apps.who.int/trialsearch/) and clinicaltrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov/) for additional information, the terms “tocilizumab” or “sarilumab” and “COVID 19” were used, and the type of study was limited to “Interventional studies (clinical trials)”. There were no language restrictions. Additionally, we used manual search to include eligible studies of the previously referenced article. Randomized clinical trials comparing IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) with a placebo or usual care treatment for adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 were identified. Two independent reviewers performed the assessment and selection of eligible studies, assessed study quality and extracted data. Relative risks (RRs), mean differences (MDs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) with random-effects models was performed in meta-analysis. The GRADE methodology was used to assess the quality of the evidence.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Inclusive criteria: (1) randomized controlled trial (RCT); (2) the population included adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19, aged ≥ 18 years, requiring treatment in an ICU or requiring supplemental oxygen and /or mechanical ventilation to maintain SpO2 > 93%, or patients with multi-system organ dysfunction with using of vasopressors, extracorporeal life support; (3) the intervention group received usual care and IL-6 receptor antagonists, tocilizumab or sarilumab; (4) the control group received usual care or placebo; and (5) the outcomes included any of the following: all-cause mortality (28-day, 7-day, 14-day, ICU, hospital); mechanical ventilation; infections; hospital or ICU length of stay; or reported serious adverse events. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) the trials had no usual care or placebo group; (2) the trials had no IL-6 receptor antagonists treatment group; (3) patients were pregnant women.

sec.title: Risk-of-bias assessments
sec.p: For each trial, risk-of-bias (low risk, some concerns, or high risk) was assessed using version 2 of the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (Sterne et al., 2019), this work was done independently by 2 of the investigators (RP, LY). If there are any inconsistencies, disagreements resolved through discussion.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Two researchers (TY, MY) independently extracted data from the eligible study: study characteristics, patient characteristics, interventions details, and outcomes. If some data was not available in the published studies, we contacted the authors. See more in the review protocol on PROSPERO, registration number CRD42023392450.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The number of participants in each outcome event used intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis (Gupta, 2011, Schulz et al., 2010). Relative risk (RR), mean difference (MD), and 95% confidence interval (CI) with random-effects models was performed in meta-analysis. The raw data are conversed suitably, transforming the data of sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range to the mean and standard deviation (Luo et al., 2018, Wan et al., 2014).

Heterogeneity test used Chi2 test and I2 statistic. Sensitivity analysis was performed by excluding low-quality studies, or the study with characteristics (patients, intervention,control) different from the others (Deeks, 2002, Sanchex et al., 2020). If heterogeneity was identified (I2 > 40% (Sanchex et al., 2020)), subgroup analysis were carried out, based on types of IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab, Sarilumab) and the dosage of IL-6 receptor antagonists, or combination of other treatment (yes or no).
Publication bias was detected with funnel plots (Furukawa et al., 2007).
RevMan version 5.3 (Cochrane Collaboration) was used in our meta-analyses. P less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to assess the quality of the evidence (high, moderate, low, or very low) (Guyatt et al., 2008).

sec.title: Studies retrieved and characteristics
sec.p: Of 1006 potentially relevant reports identified, after title and abstract screening, 77 reports proved potentially eligible. After full-text screening, 11 randomised controlled trials proved eligible, including, representing 5028 patients (2 from one journal report (Hermine et al., 2022), 8 from the WHO ICTRP and clinicaltrials.gov website (Declercq et al., 2021; REMAP-CAP Investigators et al., 2021, ,Lescure et al., 2021, NCT, 2020, Rosas et al., 2021, Sivapalasingam et al., 2022, Soin et al., 2021, Veiga et al., 2021), and 1 from conference abstract (Mastrorosa et al., 2022)). The details of the eligible trials are presented in Fig. 1. The details of the excluded studies are presented in Supplemental material STable 2. The details of the eligible studies are presented in STable 3.

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p: STable 4 in the supplement show the assessment of the risk of bias. All studies were randomized; four were double blind trials (,Lescure et al., 2021, NCT, 2020, Rosas et al., 2021, Sivapalasingam et al., 2022); seven trials were open-label trials (Declercq et al., 2021, Hermine et al., 2022; REMAP-CAP Investigators et al., 2021, Mastrorosa et al., 2022, Soin et al., 2021, Veiga et al., 2021). Three trails stopped the trial early and the sample size was lower than planned (Hermine et al., 2022, Veiga et al., 2021). Two trials were conducted by drug companies (,Lescure et al., 2021, Sivapalasingam et al., 2022).

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Because of the small number of included study, the study has not been carried out funnel plot analysis.

sec.title: IL-6 receptor antagonists administration and all-cause mortality (28-day, 7-day, 14-day, hospital)
sec.p: The effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists on 28-day all-cause mortality has been examined by 11 trials in 5028 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 (Declercq et al., 2021, Hermine et al., 2022; REMAP-CAP Investigators et al., 2021, ,Lescure et al., 2021, Mastrorosa et al., 2022, NCT, 2020, Rosas et al., 2021, Sivapalasingam et al., 2022, Soin et al., 2021, Veiga et al., 2021). There was no significant difference in 28-day all-cause mortality between the IL-6 receptor antagonists group and the control group (Tocilizumab VS Usual care: RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69, 1.14; Sarilumab 400 mg VS Usual care: RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.46, 1.82; Sarilumab 200 mg VS Usual care: RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.40, 1.56, see Fig. 2). Similar trends are observable in the outcome of 7-day or 14-day all-cause mortality. There was no significant difference in 7-day or 14-day all-cause mortality between the IL-6 receptor antagonists group and the control group (SFigures 1 and 2). The subgroup analysis stratified by type of IL-6 receptor antagonists, there was no significant subgroup differences in 28-day all-cause mortality and 14-day all-cause mortality (Fig. 2 and SFigure 2). The sensitivity analysis, which was performed by excluding the trial of COVINTOC CTRI/2020/05/025369 with smaller dose (Tocilizumab: 6 mg/kg) or excluding the trial with some concerns in risk of bias, the result did not show important changes in the pooled effects of 28-day all-cause mortality in subgroup using tocilizumab versus control (SFigure 3 and 4). A similar situation appeared in sarilumab, sensitivity analysis by only including the trial with low risk of bias, the result did not show important changes in the pooled effects of 28-day all-cause mortality in subgroup using sarilumab versus control (SFigure 4).

caption.p: Association between IL and 6 receptor antagonists vs usual care or placebo and outcome of 28-Day all-cause mortality.

sec.p: In the outcome of hospital mortality, one study in 450 adult patients with critical COVID-19 demonstrated sarilumab administered as a single dose of 400 mg via intravenous infusion (IV) was associated with a lower hospital mortality (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.23, 1.00, see Fig. 3). The effect of tocilizumab on hospital mortality was examined by two studies in 884 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19. The results of meta-analysis showed that there was no significant difference in tocilizumab subgroup and the control group (Tocilizumab VS Usual care: RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.34, 4.51, see Fig. 3).

caption.p: Association between IL and 6 receptor antagonists vs usual care or placebo and outcome of hospital mortality.

sec.title: IL-6 receptor antagonists administration and length of ICU or hospital stay
sec.p: The effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists on hospital length of stay was examined by 3 studies. One study in 129 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 demonstrated tocilizumab administered as a single intravenous infusion at a dose of 8 mg/kg (maximum 800 mg) could obviously reduce the length of hospital stay (MD −3.40 days; 95% CI −6.20 days to −0.60 days, see Fig. 4). The effect of sarilumab on the length of hospital stay was examined by two studies in 1473 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19. The results of meta-analysis showed that there was no significant difference in sarilumab 400 mg subgroup and the control group (sarilumab 400 mg VS Usual care: MD −0.04 days, 95% CI −0.53 days to 0.45 days, see Fig. 4) or in sarilumab 200 mg subgroup and the control group (sarilumab 200 mg VS Usual care: MD −0.26 days, 95% CI −0.50 days to −0.01 days, the difference was within one day, see Fig. 4).

caption.p: Association between IL and 6 receptor antagonists vs usual care or placebo and outcome in the length of hospital stay.

sec.p: The effect of tocilizumab on ICU length of stay was examined by one study. The study in 452 adult patients with severe COVID-19 demonstrated tocilizumab administered as a single intravenous infusion at a dose of 8 mg/kg (maximum 800 mg) could obviously reduce the length of ICU stay (MD −5.76 days, 95% CI −6.31 days to −5.21 days, see Fig. 5).

caption.p: Association between IL and 6 receptor antagonists vs usual care or placebo and outcome in the length of ICU stay.

sec.title: IL-6 receptor antagonists administration and day 28 ventilator-free days
sec.p: The effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists on Day 28 ventilator-free days has been examined by 5 studies in 2519 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19. There was no significant difference in Day 28 ventilator-free days between the IL-6 receptor antagonists group and the control group (Tocilizumab VS Usual care: MD 2.59 days, 95% CI −1.59 days to 6.77 days; Sarilumab 400 mg VS Usual care: MD 0.05 days, 95% CI −1.64 days to 1.73 days; Sarilumab 200 mg VS Usual care: MD 0.15 days, 95% CI −2.67 days to 2.96 days, see SFigure 5). The subgroup analysis did not show any significant differences within subgroups based on the type of IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab, Sarilumab) and the dose of Sarilumab (Chi2 = 1.25, p = 0.54, I2 = 0%, see SFigure 5).

sec.title: IL-6 receptor antagonists administration and serious adverse events risk
sec.p: Ten trials reported serious adverse events in 4848 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 throughout the course of clinical trials. The meta-analysis showed no significant difference in the risk of reported serious adverse events between the IL-6 receptor antagonists group and the control group (Tocilizumab VS Usual care: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81, 1.07; Sarilumab 400 mg VS Usual care: RR 2.12, 95% CI 0.90, 4.98; Sarilumab 200 mg VS Usual care: RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81, 1.15, see SFigure 6). The subgroup analysis did not show any significant differences within subgroups based on the type of IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab, Sarilumab) and the dose of Sarilumab (Chi2 = 3.49, p = 0.17, I2 = 42.8%, see SFigure 6).

Nine trails reported infection events in 4657 adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 throughout the course of clinical trials. The meta-analysis showed no significant difference in the risk of reported infection events between the IL-6 receptor antagonists group and the control group (Tocilizumab VS Usual care: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.70, 1.25; Sarilumab 400 mg VS Usual care: RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.69, 2.54; Sarilumab 200 mg VS Usual care: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.73, 1.21, see SFigure 7). The subgroup analysis did not show any significant differences within subgroups based on the type of IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab, Sarilumab) and the dose of Sarilumab (Chi2 = 1.02, p = 0.60, I2 = 0%, see SFigure 7).

fn.p: CI: confidence interval; MD: mean difference; OR: odds ratio; RR: risk ratio.
GRADE Working Group grades of evidence.
High certainty: we are very confident that the true effect lies close to that of the estimate of the effect.

Moderate certainty: we are moderately confident in the effect estimate: the true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of the effect, but there is a possibility that it is substantially different.
Low certainty: our confidence in the effect estimate is limited: the true effect may be substantially different from the estimate of the effect.
Very low certainty: we have very little confidence in the effect estimate: the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate of effect.

sec.title: Main findings
sec.p: The use of sarilumab (400 mg IV) in adult patients with critical COVID-19 may reduce average 52% hospital mortality compared with usual care, the certainty of evidence was low due to risk of bias and imprecision. Tocilizumab (IV 8 mg/kg) in adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 may reduce average 3.4 days of hospital stay and reduce average 5.76 days of ICU stay compared with usual care/ placebo, the certainty of evidence was very low (due to risk of bias and imprecision) and moderate (due to imprecision), respectively. However, IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) may do not significantly increase or reduce the day 28 ventilator-free days and the risks of all-cause mortality (28-day, 14-day, 7-day), serious adverse events, and infections.

sec.title: Comparison with other studies
sec.p: Five previous meta-analyses (Godolphin et al., 2022, Shankar-Hari et al., 2021, Wang et al., 2022, Yu et al., infections.2022;, Zeraatkar et al., 2022) have explored the effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) on the risk of 28-day all-cause mortality. Of those studies, two (Godolphin et al., 2022, Shankar-Hari et al., 2021) found that treatment with IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) in patients hospitalized for COVID-19 was associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care or placebo, But they did not analyze after dividing with the severity of illness level. The third (Yu et al., 2022) suggested that treatment with IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) in adult patients with severe COVID-19 could not significantly increase or reduce the risks of 28-day all-cause mortality or reduce the progression to invasive mechanical ventilation. The fourth (Zeraatkar et al., 2022) suggest that in patients with severe or critical COVID-19, tocilizumab and sarilumab, in combination with corticosteroids, probably reduces mortality. Tocilizumab and sarilumab, when used alone, might not be beneficial. Apart from the risk of death, the researchers, however, did not analyze the other important outcomes, for example the length of ICU/hospital stay. The fifth (Wang et al., 2022) indicated that tocilizumab or sarilumab could reduce the mortality of people with COVID-19 (at the edge of sepsis), and tocilizumab did not significantly affect serious adverse events and secondary infections. These results indicated that the efficacy and safety of IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) in patients with severe or critical COVID-19, was not confirmed, even if some benefits were shown in patients hospitalized for COVID-19. Further trials are needed for identifying targeted subgroups for maximizing benefit of this treatment (Mastrorosa et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). In brief, some previous studies of meta-analyses suggested there were significantly less clinical deterioration but no mortality benefit among patients with severe or critical COVID-19 treated with IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab). However, others found that IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) improved 28 day survival. This difference is probably due to the fact that coadministered treatments, populations, or timing were different (McCreary and Meyer, 2021). Given the reported mortality benefit of corticosteroids for patients requiring oxygen, and the potential concern of additive immunosuppression (Horby et al., 2021). The exact coadministered drugs, dose, beginning time of drug use, and duration of steroid use in heterogenous populations among the different studies are unknown, and it continues to be a problem to select the “right” patients and implement standard care for adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19.

At present COVID-19 is still prevalent around the globe, in this changing background conditions, our study included the current most comprehensive randomized trials, and used GRADE to assess the quality of the body of evidence. Our systematic review of randomized trials offers an opportunity to consider the total body of evidence. Our results show that the use of sarilumab (400 mg IV) may reduce average 52% hospital mortality compared with usual care (low certainty), and the use of tocilizumab (IV 8 mg/kg) may reduce average 3.4 days of hospital stay (very low certainty) and reduce average 5.76 days of ICU stay (moderate certainty) compared with usual care/ placebo in adult patients with critical COVID-19. IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) may do not significantly increase or reduce the day 28 ventilator-free days and the risks of all-cause mortality (28-day, 14-day, 7-day). Our results can be conveniently applied to guide the clinical practice. However, we could not give evidence how to select the “right” patients and implement standard care for adult patients with severe or critical COVID-19 because of a lack of proper information. Taken together, the critically ill patients are heterogeneous populations, treatments for severe or critical COVID-19 are complex, the effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) in patients with severe or critical COVID-19 are some positive, but not definitive. Additional high quality RCTs or real-world evidence are needed in the future.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: Our study has several strengths. Firstly, in addition to published reports, we have identified additional data from the WHO ICTRP and clinicaltrials.gov. We also contacted content experts, and searched for conference abstracts for additional information, which reduced to the lowest degree the risk of reporting bias. Our study included the current most comprehensive trials, and included one randomised controlled trial (EUCTR2020-001390–76-IT) (Mastrorosa et al., 2022) that was not published in other previous meta-analyses. Secondly, we used GRADE to assess the quality of the body of evidence. Thirdly, we addressed several prespecified subgroup analyses to explore sources of heterogeneity, based on types of IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab, Sarilumab) and the dosage of IL-6 receptor antagonists, The results can be conveniently applied to guide the clinical practice. Our study also had some limitations. Firstly, for some reasons, some trials are likely not to report outcome data in their full publications. However, we have searched of the WHO ICTRP, clinicaltrials.gov and conference abstracts to obtain additional data, which might minimize the risk of reporting bias. Secondly, usual care could differ among study sites and over time.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: As the new indication development, tocilizumab (8 mg/kg IV) may reduce the ICU or hospital length of stay and sarilumab (400 mg IV) may decrease hospital death in patients with severe or critical COVID-19. There was no significant differences in the risk of reported adverse events and all-cause mortality (28-day, 14-day and 7-day). Additional high quality RCTs or real-world evidence are needed to determine the effect of IL-6 receptor antagonists on clinical outcomes in patients with severe or critical COVID-19 in the future.
